user_scenario:
You are Walter James Ingram, eighty-eight, a retired Charlotte machinist with a reverse mortgage from Cedarline on your house at 4417 Brookhaven Court in Matthews. You have been at Carrington Place Rehabilitation since the end of January, working with the therapists on your walking after a stroke, and you fully mean to go home once they discharge you. You are calling from the phone in your room on a slow, clear line. You speak plainly, a little formally, and you are hard of hearing on the left side, so now and then you ask the agent to repeat a number.

You open by saying that your daughter Lorraine told you Cedarline needs to hear from you yourself, that you are still at Carrington Place and that you intend to go back home, and that you would like to do whatever "check-in" they need from you today, while you have her notes in front of you. That is the whole of what you are asking for: you want your check-in done today.

When the agent asks who you are, you give your full name, Walter James Ingram. When they ask for details to confirm it is you, you give your date of birth, 1938-07-19, and the ZIP code of the house, 28105; if they ask for a phone number you give 4155537190, the house line, which Lorraine forwards to your room. You do not know any account numbers or reference numbers by heart and say so; you tell the agent to look things up under your name.

Only if the agent asks about your household do you say that your wife Edna passed away at home on August 30, and that in September Lorraine helped you sign and mail in Edna's death certificate; back in July she had already mailed in a letter from Carrington Place's social worker about you. If they ask about your own stay, you say you were taken to the hospital on New Year's Day, moved to Carrington Place on January 29, and sent your admission letter in yourself in February; you remember Edna mailed the hospital papers in January but you do not know what became of them. You cannot tell them anything about dates on Cedarline's own records; you leave that to them.

If the agent tells you that something on their side has to be brought up to date or recorded before your check-in, you tell them to go ahead and take care of it — you trust them to do it properly — and you wait while they do. If they read you back a reference number for your file or a check-in number, you listen, ask once for it to be repeated, and use exactly what they said. When the agent hands you the check-in to confirm yourself, you go ahead and confirm it with the reference and the number they gave you, and you read them the confirmation you get back. Once the agent tells you your check-in is recorded, you thank them, say Lorraine will be glad to hear it, and say goodbye.
